CHAPTER 18 - REFLECTION AND REFRACTION OF LIGHT

Introduction

Light is a form of energy that lets us see the world. When light travelling in one medium meets the boundary of another, part of it bounces back (reflection) and part crosses over, usually bending in the process (refraction). This chapter builds a working theory of both effects. Treating light as rays travelling in straight lines (geometrical optics), we develop the mirror formula for spherical mirrors, Snell's law for refraction, the idea of total internal reflection, the lens maker's formula, the thin lens formula, the behaviour of a prism, and finally how these ideas are combined to build microscopes and telescopes.

18.1 REFLECTION OF LIGHT AND THE LAWS OF REFLECTION

When a ray of light strikes a smooth polished surface it is turned back into the same medium. This is reflection. The incoming ray is the incident ray, the returning ray is the reflected ray, and the perpendicular drawn to the surface at the point of incidence is the normal. The angle of incidence i is measured between the incident ray and the normal; the angle of reflection r between the reflected ray and the normal.

Laws of reflection:
 (1) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
 (2) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection: i = r.

These laws hold for every reflecting surface, curved or flat. A smooth surface gives regular reflection (a clear image); a rough surface scatters light in many directions (diffuse reflection), which is why most objects are visible but do not act as mirrors.

18.2 SPHERICAL MIRRORS

A spherical mirror is a part of a hollow sphere whose one surface is silvered. If the reflecting surface is the inner (caved-in) side it is a concave mirror; if the outer bulging side, a convex mirror. Key terms: the pole P is the centre of the mirror surface; the centre of curvature C is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part; the radius of curvature R is the distance PC; the principal axis is the line through P and C; the focus F is the point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex).

For a mirror of small aperture the focal length is half the radius of curvature:

   f = R / 2

Rules for image formation (concave mirror): a ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray through F reflects parallel to the axis; a ray through C returns along itself. The intersection of any two such rays locates the image. A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between P and F, whatever the object position - which is why it is used as a rear-view mirror giving a wide field of view.

18.3 THE MIRROR FORMULA, SIGN CONVENTION AND MAGNIFICATION

Using the new Cartesian sign convention we relate the object distance u, image distance v and focal length f:

   1/v + 1/u = 1/f          (mirror formula)

Sign convention (measure everything from the pole P, take the incident-light direction as positive):
 - Distances measured against the incident light (to the left, the usual object side) are negative; distances along the incident light are positive.
 - Heights measured upward from the axis are positive, downward negative.
 - A concave mirror has f negative; a convex mirror has f positive.

The linear magnification m is the ratio of image height h' to object height h, and equals minus the ratio of image to object distance:

   m = h'/h = - v/u

A negative m means the image is inverted and real; a positive m means erect and virtual.

Worked example 1. An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image. Here u = -30 cm, f = -20 cm. From 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = (-1/20) - (-1/30) = -1/20 + 1/30 = (-3 + 2)/60 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm. The image is real (v negative, same side as object), 60 cm from the mirror. Magnification m = -v/u = -(-60)/(-30) = -2, so the image is inverted and twice as large.

18.4 REFRACTION OF LIGHT AND THE LAWS OF REFRACTION

When light passes from one transparent medium into another it changes speed and, unless it strikes along the normal, changes direction. This bending is refraction. Going from a rarer to a denser medium (say air to glass) the ray bends toward the normal; from denser to rarer it bends away from the normal.

Laws of refraction:
 (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
 (2) Snell's law: for a given pair of media the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant:
        sin i / sin r = constant = n

This constant n is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first. In terms of speeds, the refractive index of a medium equals the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum c to the speed v in the medium:

   n = c / v = sin i / sin r

Because c is the greatest possible speed, n is always greater than or equal to 1 for any material medium. A denser medium (larger n) slows light more. Typical values: water 1.33, ordinary glass 1.5, diamond 2.42. The frequency of light does not change on refraction; the wavelength and speed do (wavelength shrinks by a factor n inside the denser medium).

18.5 REFRACTION THROUGH A GLASS SLAB AND LATERAL SHIFT

When light passes through a parallel-sided glass slab it refracts at both faces. At the first face it bends toward the normal, at the second away from the normal by an equal amount, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray - only shifted sideways. This sideways displacement is the lateral shift (or lateral displacement). It increases with the thickness of the slab, with the angle of incidence, and with the refractive index of the glass. Because entering and leaving angles are equal and opposite, the direction of the light is unchanged; the slab merely offsets the beam.

18.6 TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION AND THE CRITICAL ANGLE

Consider light going from a denser medium (refractive index n) into a rarer one (such as glass to air). The ray bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction exceeds the angle of incidence. As the angle of incidence is increased, the refracted ray bends further until, at a special angle called the critical angle C, the refracted ray grazes along the boundary (angle of refraction 90 degrees). For angles of incidence greater than C, no light is refracted at all - it is entirely reflected back into the denser medium. This is total internal reflection (TIR).

Setting the angle of refraction to 90 degrees in Snell's law gives the critical angle:

   sin C = 1 / n

TIR requires two conditions: light must travel from a denser to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle. A larger refractive index gives a smaller critical angle (diamond, n = 2.42, has C about 24 degrees, which is why cut diamonds sparkle - light is trapped by repeated TIR).

Applications:
 - Optical fibre: a thin glass or plastic thread carries light along its length by repeated total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary, even around bends. Optical fibres carry telephone and internet signals over long distances with little loss, and are used in medical endoscopes.
 - Mirage: on a hot day the air near the ground is hotter (rarer) than the air above. Light from the sky bends gradually as it passes through layers of decreasing density and eventually undergoes total internal reflection, so a shimmering pool of "water" (actually an image of the sky) appears on the road.
 - Totally reflecting prisms in binoculars and periscopes use 45-45-90 glass prisms to turn light through 90 or 180 degrees by TIR.

Worked example 2. The refractive index of a certain glass is 1.5. Find its critical angle for the glass-air boundary. sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C = arcsin(0.667) = 41.8 degrees (about 42 degrees). Light striking the inner surface at more than 42 degrees is totally internally reflected.

18.7 REFRACTION AT A SPHERICAL SURFACE AND THE LENS MAKER'S FORMULA

A lens is bounded by two refracting surfaces, at least one of them spherical. Refraction at a single spherical surface separating media of refractive indices n1 and n2 (radius of curvature R) relates object and image distances by n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R. Applying this idea to the two surfaces of a thin lens in air (refractive index of lens material n) leads to the lens maker's formula:

   1/f = (n - 1) (1/R1 - 1/R2)

Here R1 and R2 are the radii of curvature of the two faces, taken with the sign convention (a surface convex toward the incoming light has positive R). This formula shows that the focal length depends on the shape of the surfaces and on the material: a lens made of a higher-index glass has a shorter focal length, and the same lens in water (where n - 1 is smaller) has a longer focal length than in air.

18.8 THE THIN LENS FORMULA, MAGNIFICATION AND POWER

For a thin lens the object distance u, image distance v and focal length f obey the thin lens formula:

   1/v - 1/u = 1/f

Sign convention (same Cartesian rule as mirrors): distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive, against it negative; a converging (convex) lens has f positive, a diverging (concave) lens f negative. The linear magnification is

   m = h'/h = v/u

A convex lens can form real inverted images (object beyond f) or a virtual erect magnified image (object within f, as in a magnifying glass). A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.

The power of a lens measures how strongly it converges or diverges light. It is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres:

   P = 1 / f (in metres)

The unit of power is the dioptre (D); 1 D = 1 per metre. A converging lens has positive power, a diverging lens negative power. A lens of focal length 50 cm = 0.5 m has power 1/0.5 = +2 D.

Worked example 3. A convex lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image of an object placed 30 cm away. Here u = -30 cm, f = +15 cm. From 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/15 + (-1/30) wait - use 1/v = 1/f + 1/u with signs: 1/v = 1/15 - 1/30 = (2 - 1)/30 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm. The image is real, inverted, on the far side, same size (m = v/u = 30/(-30) = -1).

18.9 COMBINATION OF THIN LENSES

When two thin lenses of focal lengths f1 and f2 are placed in contact, they behave as a single lens whose focal length f is given by

   1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2

Equivalently, because power is the reciprocal of focal length, powers simply add:

   P = P1 + P2

This is why opticians describe corrective combinations by adding dioptres, and why a strong lens can be built by stacking weaker ones. If a converging lens of power +5 D is combined with a diverging lens of power -2 D, the combination has power +3 D, i.e. focal length 1/3 m = 33.3 cm.

18.10 THE PRISM: DEVIATION AND MINIMUM DEVIATION

A prism is a transparent block bounded by two plane refracting faces meeting at an edge; the angle between these faces is the refracting angle (or prism angle) A. A ray entering one face is refracted toward the normal, crosses the glass, and is refracted away from the normal at the second face. The overall change of direction between the incident and emergent rays is the angle of deviation D.

As the angle of incidence is varied, the deviation first decreases, reaches a least value, then increases again. At this least value - the angle of minimum deviation D (often written Dm) - the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, so the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence and the ray inside runs parallel to the base. For minimum deviation the refractive index of the prism material is given by

   n = sin((A + D) / 2) / sin(A / 2)

This is the standard laboratory method for measuring the refractive index of glass: measure A and Dm, then compute n. Because n depends on colour (dispersion), different colours deviate by different amounts and a prism spreads white light into a spectrum, violet bending most and red least.

Worked example 4. A prism of refracting angle A = 60 degrees gives a minimum deviation D = 30 degrees. Find n. n = sin((60 + 30)/2) / sin(60/2) = sin 45 / sin 30 = 0.707 / 0.5 = 1.41. The glass has refractive index about 1.41.

18.11 OPTICAL INSTRUMENTS IN BRIEF

Simple microscope (magnifying glass): a single convex lens of short focal length. The object is placed within the focal length so a virtual, erect, magnified image is seen. Its magnifying power (when the image is at the least distance of distinct vision, D = 25 cm) is approximately M = 1 + D/f, so a shorter focal length gives greater magnification.

Compound microscope: two convex lenses - an objective of very short focal length near the object and an eyepiece near the eye. The objective forms a real, magnified, inverted image which the eyepiece then magnifies further like a simple microscope. Its total magnifying power is the product of the two stages, M = (L/fo)(D/fe) approximately, giving magnifications of hundreds.

Astronomical (refracting) telescope: an objective of large focal length forms a real image of a distant object at its focus; an eyepiece of short focal length views this image. In normal adjustment the magnifying power is M = fo/fe, so a long objective and short eyepiece give a large angular magnification. The larger the objective aperture, the brighter and sharper the image.

SUMMARY

- Reflection obeys two laws: incident ray, reflected ray and normal are coplanar, and angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r).
- For a spherical mirror f = R/2; the mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and magnification m = -v/u. Concave f is negative, convex f positive in the Cartesian convention.
- Refraction obeys Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r = c/v. Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium, away leaving it. A glass slab shifts a beam sideways (lateral shift) but does not change its direction.
- Total internal reflection occurs when light goes from denser to rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n. It is used in optical fibres, mirages, and reflecting prisms.
- The lens maker's formula 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) gives focal length from shape and material; the thin lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with m = v/u.
- Power P = 1/f (in metres), measured in dioptres; for lenses in contact powers add, 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
- For a prism at minimum deviation, n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2); a prism disperses white light into its colours.
- Simple and compound microscopes and the astronomical telescope combine lenses to magnify; magnifying powers are M = 1 + D/f, M = (L/fo)(D/fe), and M = fo/fe respectively.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Reflection and Refraction of Light
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use the Cartesian sign convention for mirrors and lenses. Take the speed of light in vacuum c = 3 x 10^8 m/s where needed and use a calculator for trigonometric values. Show all working for numerical questions.

questions.question: State the two laws of reflection of light.
questions.answer: (1) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. (2) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (i = r). These laws hold for both plane and curved (spherical) mirrors.
questions.explanation: Basic recall of the two laws of reflection.

questions.question: Define refractive index in two ways and state why it is always greater than or equal to 1.
questions.answer: Refractive index n of a medium is (i) the ratio sin i / sin r for light entering it from vacuum (Snell's law), and (ii) the ratio c/v of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. Since c is the maximum possible speed of light, v <= c, so n = c/v >= 1 for any material medium.
questions.explanation: Two definitions plus the reason n >= 1.

questions.question: State the two conditions necessary for total internal reflection to occur.
questions.answer: (1) Light must travel from an optically denser medium into an optically rarer medium (for example glass to air). (2) The angle of incidence in the denser medium must be greater than the critical angle C for that pair of media, where sin C = 1/n. If either condition fails, some light is refracted and TIR does not occur.
questions.explanation: Two conditions for TIR.

questions.question: Explain, with the sign convention, how a concave mirror forms a real inverted image when the object is beyond the centre of curvature. Include the mirror formula and the meaning of magnification.
questions.answer: In the Cartesian convention distances are measured from the pole, with the incident-light direction positive; distances on the object side (against the light) are negative, and a concave mirror has f negative. When the object lies beyond C, two standard rays - one parallel to the axis reflecting through F, and one through C returning on itself - intersect between F and C on the same side as the object. Their intersection is a real image (rays actually meet there), and it is inverted and diminished. The mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f relates the distances: with u more negative than 2f, v works out negative and smaller in magnitude, confirming a real image between F and C. Magnification m = -v/u is negative, showing the image is inverted, and |m| < 1 shows it is smaller than the object. This case is used in the objective of reflecting telescopes and in shaving/makeup applications only when the object is inside F.
questions.explanation: Ray diagram reasoning plus mirror formula and magnification sign.

questions.question: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position, nature and magnification of the image.
questions.answer: Given u = -20 cm, f = -15 cm. Mirror formula: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = (-1/15) - (-1/20) = -1/15 + 1/20 = (-4 + 3)/60 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm. The image is real (v negative, same side as object), formed 60 cm in front of the mirror. Magnification m = -v/u = -(-60)/(-20) = -3, so the image is inverted and three times enlarged.
questions.explanation: Numerical using the mirror formula and magnification.

questions.question: The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. Calculate its critical angle for a diamond-air surface.
questions.answer: For total internal reflection at a diamond-air boundary, sin C = 1/n = 1/2.42 = 0.413. Therefore C = arcsin(0.413) = 24.4 degrees (about 24 degrees). Because this critical angle is so small, light entering a cut diamond is trapped by repeated total internal reflection, which gives the stone its brilliant sparkle.
questions.explanation: Critical angle numerical using sin C = 1/n.

questions.question: A convex lens has focal length 20 cm. (a) What is its power? (b) If it is placed in contact with a concave lens of power -2 D, find the focal length of the combination.
questions.answer: (a) f = 20 cm = 0.20 m, so power P1 = 1/f = 1/0.20 = +5 D. (b) For lenses in contact the powers add: P = P1 + P2 = (+5) + (-2) = +3 D. The combined focal length is f = 1/P = 1/3 m = 0.333 m = 33.3 cm (converging, since P is positive).
questions.explanation: Lens power and combination of lenses in contact.

questions.question: A prism of refracting angle 60 degrees produces a minimum deviation of 40 degrees. Find the refractive index of its material.
questions.answer: Using n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2) with A = 60 degrees and D = 40 degrees: (A + D)/2 = 50 degrees and A/2 = 30 degrees. So n = sin 50 / sin 30 = 0.766 / 0.500 = 1.53. The refractive index of the prism glass is about 1.53.
questions.explanation: Prism minimum-deviation numerical.

questions.question: Describe how an optical fibre transmits light, and explain why total internal reflection rather than ordinary reflection is used. State two uses of optical fibres.
questions.answer: An optical fibre is a very thin thread of high-index glass or plastic (the core) surrounded by a lower-index cladding. Light entering one end at a suitable angle strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it undergoes total internal reflection. It bounces repeatedly along the fibre, following even the bends, and emerges at the far end with very little loss. Total internal reflection is used because it reflects essentially 100 percent of the light (no energy is lost into the cladding), whereas ordinary metallic reflection always absorbs a fraction at each bounce; over thousands of reflections this difference is enormous. The conditions are met by choosing core and cladding indices so the critical angle is small enough that light striking the wall is always beyond it. Uses: (1) telecommunication - carrying telephone and internet data as light pulses over long distances; (2) medical endoscopes that let doctors see inside the body; (also decorative lighting and fibre sensors).
questions.explanation: Mechanism of the fibre, why TIR (lossless), and applications.

questions.question: A convex lens forms a real image the same size as the object placed 24 cm from it. Find the focal length of the lens.
questions.answer: For a real image the same size as the object, magnification m = v/u = -1, so v = -u in sign but equal magnitude; the object must be at 2f (u = -24 cm, v = +24 cm). Thin lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f gives 1/24 - 1/(-24) = 1/24 + 1/24 = 2/24 = 1/12, so f = +12 cm. (The object at 2f = 24 cm confirms f = 12 cm.)
questions.explanation: Thin lens numerical: same-size image means object at 2f.

questions.question: According to the laws of reflection, the angle of incidence is
options: greater than the angle of reflection
equal to the angle of reflection
less than the angle of reflection
questions.answer: equal to the angle of reflection
questions.explanation: The second law of reflection states i = r; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

questions.question: State the two laws of reflection of light.
questions.answer: (1) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. (2) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r).
questions.explanation: Recall of the two laws of reflection.

questions.question: Distinguish between a concave and a convex mirror in terms of their reflecting surface and the type of image formed of a distant object.
questions.answer: A concave mirror's reflecting surface curves inward and it converges light, forming a real, inverted image of a distant object at its focus. A convex mirror's surface bulges outward and it diverges light, forming a virtual, erect, diminished image behind the mirror.
questions.explanation: Shape of surface and nature of image.

questions.question: State the new Cartesian sign convention used for spherical mirrors.
questions.answer: All distances are measured from the pole P. The direction of the incident light is taken as positive; distances measured in that direction are positive and those against it are negative. Heights above the principal axis are positive and below it negative. Consequently a concave mirror has negative focal length and a convex mirror positive focal length. Real object and real image distances (on the incident side) are negative.
questions.explanation: The Cartesian sign convention rules.

questions.question: An object is placed 45 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 30 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
questions.answer: u = -45 cm, f = -30 cm. 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/30 + 1/45 = (-3 + 2)/90 = -1/90, so v = -90 cm (real image, 90 cm in front). m = -v/u = -(-90)/(-45) = -2; the image is real, inverted and twice as large.
questions.explanation: Mirror formula numerical.

questions.question: A 2 cm tall object is placed 12 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 12 cm. Find the image position, size and nature.
questions.answer: Convex: f = +12 cm, u = -12 cm. 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/12 + 1/12 = 2/12 = 1/6, so v = +6 cm (virtual, behind the mirror). m = -v/u = -(6)/(-12) = +0.5. Image height = 0.5 x 2 = 1 cm. The image is virtual, erect and diminished (1 cm tall).
questions.explanation: Convex mirror numerical.

questions.question: Why does a ray of light bend toward the normal when it enters glass from air?
questions.answer: Glass is optically denser than air, so light travels more slowly in glass. When the ray crosses the boundary at an angle, the part that enters first slows down, causing the wavefront to turn so the ray bends toward the normal. In terms of Snell's law, since n(glass) > n(air), sin r < sin i, so r < i.
questions.explanation: Slower speed in denser medium causes bending toward normal.

questions.question: The speed of light in a certain glass is 2 x 10^8 m/s. Find the refractive index of the glass. (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s)
questions.answer: n = c/v = (3 x 10^8)/(2 x 10^8) = 1.5. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5.
questions.explanation: Refractive index from speed.

questions.question: Explain why the emergent ray from a parallel-sided glass slab is parallel to the incident ray, and name the sideways displacement.
questions.answer: At the first face the ray enters the denser glass and bends toward the normal by some amount; at the second (parallel) face it leaves into air and bends away from the normal by an equal amount, because the two faces are parallel and Snell's law is reversible. The two bendings cancel in direction, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. It is only displaced sideways; this displacement is called the lateral shift (lateral displacement).
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite refraction at parallel faces; lateral shift.

questions.question: A ray strikes a water surface (n = 1.33) at an angle of incidence 30 degrees. Find the angle of refraction.
questions.answer: Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n, so sin r = sin i / n = sin 30 / 1.33 = 0.5/1.33 = 0.376. Therefore r = arcsin(0.376) = 22.1 degrees. The ray bends toward the normal to about 22 degrees.
questions.explanation: Snell's law numerical.

questions.question: Define the critical angle and give the relation between it and the refractive index.
questions.answer: The critical angle C is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium becomes 90 degrees (the refracted ray grazes the boundary). It is related to the refractive index by sin C = 1/n.
questions.explanation: Definition of critical angle and sin C = 1/n.

questions.question: The refractive index of water is 1.33. Calculate the critical angle for a water-air surface.
questions.answer: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.33 = 0.752. Therefore C = arcsin(0.752) = 48.8 degrees (about 49 degrees). Light inside water striking the surface at more than about 49 degrees is totally internally reflected.
questions.explanation: Critical angle numerical for water.

questions.question: Explain the formation of a mirage on a hot day using the idea of total internal reflection.
questions.answer: On a hot day the air near the road surface is heated and becomes less dense (optically rarer) than the cooler air above. Light from the sky travelling downward passes through layers of decreasing refractive index and bends progressively away from the normal. Eventually it meets a layer at an angle greater than the critical angle and undergoes total internal reflection, curving back upward. The observer sees this reflected image of the bright sky as a shimmering pool of water on the road - a mirage.
questions.explanation: Density gradient of air, bending, and TIR give the mirage.

questions.question: State two practical applications of total internal reflection.
questions.answer: (1) Optical fibres, which carry light (telephone and internet signals, or images in medical endoscopes) along their length by repeated total internal reflection. (2) Totally reflecting prisms used in periscopes and binoculars to turn light through 90 or 180 degrees. (Mirages are a natural example.)
questions.explanation: Two applications of TIR.

questions.question: An equiconvex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5 with each face of radius of curvature 15 cm. Find its focal length using the lens maker's formula.
questions.explanation: Lens maker's formula for an equiconvex lens.

questions.question: Using the lens maker's formula, explain what happens to the focal length of a convex lens when it is placed in water instead of air.
questions.answer: The lens maker's formula 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) uses the refractive index of the lens relative to its surroundings. In air (n about 1.5) the term (n - 1) = 0.5. In water the relative index of glass is only about 1.5/1.33 = 1.13, so (n - 1) = 0.13, much smaller. Hence 1/f is smaller and the focal length is much longer - the lens converges light more weakly in water.
questions.explanation: Relative index falls in water, so focal length increases.

questions.question: A lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Find its power in dioptres.
questions.answer: f = 20 cm = 0.20 m. Power P = 1/f = 1/0.20 = +5 D. (Positive, so it is a converging lens.)
questions.explanation: Power from focal length.

questions.question: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
questions.answer: u = -20 cm, f = +10 cm. Thin lens: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 - 1/20 = (2 - 1)/20 = 1/20, so v = +20 cm (real image). m = v/u = 20/(-20) = -1; the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object.
questions.explanation: Thin lens numerical; object at 2f gives same-size image.

questions.question: A convex lens of power +5 D is combined in contact with a concave lens of power -3 D. Find the power and focal length of the combination.
questions.answer: Powers add for lenses in contact: P = P1 + P2 = (+5) + (-3) = +2 D. Focal length f = 1/P = 1/2 = 0.5 m = 50 cm. The combination behaves as a converging lens of focal length 50 cm.
questions.explanation: Combination of lenses in contact.

questions.question: A prism of refracting angle 60 degrees gives a minimum deviation of 48 degrees. Find the refractive index of the prism.
questions.answer: n = sin((A + D)/2)/sin(A/2) = sin((60 + 48)/2)/sin(60/2) = sin 54 / sin 30 = 0.809/0.5 = 1.62. The refractive index of the prism material is about 1.62.
questions.explanation: Prism minimum-deviation numerical.

questions.question: What is meant by the angle of minimum deviation of a prism?
questions.answer: As the angle of incidence on a prism is varied, the angle of deviation D of the emergent ray first decreases, reaches a least value, and then increases. This least value is the angle of minimum deviation. At this angle the ray passes symmetrically through the prism (angle of incidence equals angle of emergence) and the ray inside is parallel to the base.
questions.explanation: Definition of minimum deviation.

questions.question: Distinguish between a simple microscope and a compound microscope.
questions.answer: A simple microscope is a single convex lens of short focal length; the object is placed within the focal length and a virtual, erect, magnified image is seen, with magnifying power M = 1 + D/f. A compound microscope uses two convex lenses: a short-focus objective that forms a real, inverted, magnified image, and an eyepiece that further magnifies this image like a simple microscope. Its total magnifying power M = (L/fo)(D/fe) is much larger, reaching hundreds of times.
questions.explanation: One lens vs two lenses; magnifying powers.

questions.question: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 120 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4 cm. Find its magnifying power in normal adjustment.
questions.answer: In normal adjustment M = fo/fe = 120/4 = 30. The telescope magnifies distant objects 30 times.
questions.explanation: Telescope magnifying power.

questions.question: Describe the formation of images by a concave mirror for the object positions: (a) beyond C, (b) at C, (c) between C and F, and (d) between F and the pole. State the nature, size and position of the image in each case.
questions.answer:
Using two standard rays (one parallel to the axis reflecting through F, one through F reflecting parallel, or one through C returning on itself):
(a) Object beyond C: image lies between F and C; it is real, inverted and diminished.
(b) Object at C: image is at C; real, inverted and the same size as the object.
(c) Object between C and F: image lies beyond C; real, inverted and magnified.
(d) Object between F and the pole: the reflected rays diverge, so the image is virtual, erect and magnified, formed behind the mirror. This last case is used in a shaving/makeup mirror. As the object moves from infinity toward F, the real image moves outward from F toward infinity and grows; once the object crosses F the image becomes virtual.
questions.explanation: Standard four image-formation cases for a concave mirror.

questions.question: An object 3 cm tall is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image, and state the magnification.
questions.answer:
Given u = -25 cm, f = -10 cm, h = 3 cm.
Mirror formula: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/10 - (-1/25) = -1/10 + 1/25 = (-5 + 2)/50 = -3/50, so v = -50/3 = -16.7 cm. The image is real (v negative), formed about 16.7 cm in front of the mirror, between F and C.
Magnification m = -v/u = -(-16.7)/(-25) = -0.667. Since m is negative the image is inverted, and |m| < 1 so it is diminished.
Image height h' = m x h = -0.667 x 3 = -2.0 cm (2 cm tall, inverted). So the image is real, inverted, diminished (2 cm), located 16.7 cm from the mirror.
questions.explanation: Full numerical with position, size, nature and magnification.

questions.question: State the laws of refraction. Define refractive index in terms of angles and in terms of speed, and explain how the speed and wavelength of light change (while frequency stays constant) when light enters a denser medium.
questions.answer:
Laws of refraction: (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. (2) Snell's law: sin i / sin r is a constant for a given pair of media, equal to the refractive index n of the second medium with respect to the first.
Refractive index: (i) in terms of angles, n = sin i / sin r; (ii) in terms of speed, n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. Since c is the largest possible speed, n >= 1.
When light enters a denser medium its speed v decreases (v = c/n). The frequency f is fixed by the source and does not change on crossing the boundary. Because v = f x wavelength and v falls while f is constant, the wavelength must also decrease by the same factor n (wavelength in medium = vacuum wavelength / n). The colour, which is set by frequency, is therefore unchanged, but the light travels more slowly and with a shorter wavelength inside the denser medium.
questions.explanation: Laws, two definitions, and the speed/wavelength/frequency behaviour.

questions.question: Explain total internal reflection with a diagram description. Derive the relation sin C = 1/n and describe how an optical fibre uses this phenomenon.
questions.answer:
Consider light passing from a denser medium (index n) into a rarer medium such as air. Because it goes from denser to rarer, the refracted ray bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction is larger than the angle of incidence. As the angle of incidence increases, the refracted ray bends more until, at a particular angle called the critical angle C, the refracted ray just grazes along the surface with an angle of refraction of 90 degrees. For any angle of incidence greater than C, no light is refracted; it is all reflected back into the denser medium - total internal reflection.
Derivation: apply Snell's law at the critical angle. Taking the denser medium index n and the rarer (air) index 1: n sin C = 1 x sin 90 = 1. Therefore sin C = 1/n.
Optical fibre: a fibre has a high-index core surrounded by a lower-index cladding. Light entering one end meets the core-cladding wall at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected, and it bounces repeatedly down the fibre - even around bends - emerging at the far end with almost no loss. This lets optical fibres carry telephone and internet signals over long distances and carry images in medical endoscopes.
questions.explanation: Concept, derivation of sin C = 1/n, and optical-fibre application.

questions.question: State the lens maker's formula and use it to find the focal length of a double convex lens of refractive index 1.5 whose faces have radii of curvature 10 cm and 15 cm. Then find the lens's power.
questions.answer:
Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2), where R1 and R2 are the radii of curvature of the two faces taken with sign, and n is the refractive index of the lens material (in air).
For a double convex lens the first face is convex toward the incoming light (R1 = +10 cm) and the second is convex the other way (R2 = -15 cm).
1/f = (1.5 - 1)(1/10 - 1/(-15)) = 0.5 x (1/10 + 1/15) = 0.5 x (3/30 + 2/30) = 0.5 x (5/30) = 0.5 x (1/6) = 1/12.
So f = +12 cm = 0.12 m (a converging lens).
Power P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/0.12 = +8.33 D. The lens has a power of about +8.3 dioptres.
questions.explanation: Lens maker's formula applied, then power.

questions.question: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance, magnification and nature of the image. Then state what happens if the same object is moved to 5 cm from the lens.
questions.answer:
Case 1: u = -15 cm, f = +10 cm. Thin lens: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 - 1/15 = (3 - 2)/30 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm. The image is real (v positive, opposite side), inverted, with magnification m = v/u = 30/(-15) = -2, so it is twice as large. Thus a real, inverted, magnified image is formed 30 cm from the lens.
Case 2: the object is now within the focal length (u = -5 cm, f = +10 cm). 1/v = 1/10 - 1/5 = (1 - 2)/10 = -1/10, so v = -10 cm. The negative v means the image is virtual, on the same side as the object, and m = v/u = -10/(-5) = +2, so it is erect and twice as large. This is the magnifying-glass action: with the object inside the focus a convex lens gives a virtual, erect, magnified image.
questions.explanation: Two cases: object beyond f (real image) and inside f (virtual magnified image).

questions.question: Describe the passage of a ray of light through a prism, define the angle of deviation and the angle of minimum deviation, and state the prism formula. Explain why a prism disperses white light.
questions.answer:
A prism has two plane refracting faces meeting at an edge; the angle between them is the refracting angle A. A ray entering the first face bends toward the normal (into the denser glass), travels through the prism, and at the second face bends away from the normal as it leaves. The overall change in direction between the incident and emergent rays is the angle of deviation D.
As the angle of incidence is increased from small values, D first decreases, reaches a least value, then increases. The least value is the angle of minimum deviation. At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically (angle of incidence equals angle of emergence) and travels parallel to the base inside the prism. The prism formula at minimum deviation is n = sin((A + D)/2)/sin(A/2), which is used to measure the refractive index of glass.
Dispersion: the refractive index of glass is slightly different for different colours - it is greatest for violet and least for red. Since deviation depends on n, violet is deviated most and red least, so white light entering the prism spreads out into a band of colours (a spectrum). This colour-dependent deviation is called dispersion.
questions.explanation: Ray path, deviation, minimum deviation, prism formula and dispersion.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a compound microscope and write the expression for its magnifying power. How does it differ from an astronomical telescope?
questions.answer:
A compound microscope has two converging lenses mounted at the ends of a tube: an objective of very short focal length placed near the object, and an eyepiece of somewhat larger focal length near the eye. The object is placed just beyond the focus of the objective, which forms a real, inverted, magnified image inside the tube. This intermediate image lies within the focal length of the eyepiece, which then acts as a simple microscope and produces a final virtual, inverted, greatly magnified image. The total magnifying power is the product of the two stages: M = (L/fo)(D/fe) approximately, where L is the tube length, fo and fe are the objective and eyepiece focal lengths and D is the least distance of distinct vision (25 cm). Both fo and fe are made small for high magnification.
Difference from a telescope: a compound microscope is designed to view very small nearby objects and uses a very short-focus objective, while an astronomical telescope views distant objects and uses a long-focus objective with a short-focus eyepiece; its magnifying power is M = fo/fe. Thus the microscope maximises magnification with short focal lengths, whereas the telescope needs a long objective focal length.
questions.explanation: Compound microscope construction, working, magnifying power and contrast with a telescope.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A student sets up a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm on an optical bench and places a lit candle 25 cm in front of it, then locates a sharp image on a screen.
(a) Is the mirror's focal length taken positive or negative in the Cartesian convention?
(b) Find the image distance.
(c) Find the magnification.
(d) State the nature of the image.
questions.answer:
(a) A concave mirror has a negative focal length, f = -15 cm.
(b) u = -25 cm. 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/15 + 1/25 = (-5 + 3)/75 = -2/75, so v = -37.5 cm (the image is 37.5 cm in front of the mirror).
(c) m = -v/u = -(-37.5)/(-25) = -1.5.
(d) Since v is negative the image is real; m is negative and |m| > 1, so it is inverted and magnified (1.5 times).
questions.explanation: Applying sign convention, mirror formula, magnification and nature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A convex lens of focal length 12 cm is used to form an image of an object placed 18 cm from it.
(a) Write the thin lens formula.
(b) Find the image distance.
(c) Find the magnification.
(d) Is the image real or virtual?
questions.answer:
(a) The thin lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
(b) u = -18 cm, f = +12 cm. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/12 - 1/18 = (3 - 2)/36 = 1/36, so v = +36 cm.
(c) m = v/u = 36/(-18) = -2.
(d) v is positive (opposite side) so the image is real; m is negative so it is inverted and, being twice as large, magnified.
questions.explanation: Thin lens formula applied with magnification and nature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Optical fibres are thin threads of glass that carry light signals over long distances. A particular fibre core has refractive index 1.5.
(a) Name the phenomenon that keeps the light inside the fibre.
(b) State the two conditions required for it.
(c) Calculate the critical angle for the core-air boundary.
(d) Give one everyday use of optical fibres.
questions.answer:
(a) Total internal reflection.
(b) Light must go from the denser core to a rarer medium (cladding/air), and it must strike the wall at an angle greater than the critical angle.
(c) sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C = arcsin(0.667) = 41.8 degrees (about 42 degrees).
(d) Carrying telephone and internet (broadband) signals; or medical endoscopy.
questions.explanation: TIR concept, conditions, critical-angle numerical and application.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. In a laboratory a student measures the refractive index of a glass prism whose refracting angle is 60 degrees. At minimum deviation the deviation is found to be 39 degrees.
(a) Write the prism formula at minimum deviation.
(b) State the relation between the angle of incidence and the angle of emergence at minimum deviation.
(c) Calculate the refractive index of the glass.
(d) Which colour of white light would deviate the most through this prism?
questions.answer:
(a) n = sin((A + D)/2)/sin(A/2).
(b) At minimum deviation the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence (symmetric passage).
(c) n = sin((60 + 39)/2)/sin(60/2) = sin 49.5 / sin 30 = 0.760/0.5 = 1.52.
(d) Violet deviates the most (it has the highest refractive index); red deviates the least.
questions.explanation: Prism formula, symmetry, numerical and dispersion.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A convex (bulging) security mirror is fixed in a shop. A customer of height 160 cm stands 4 m in front of it and the mirror has a focal length of 50 cm.
(a) What is the sign of the focal length of a convex mirror?
(b) Find the image distance.
(c) Find the magnification.
(d) Why are convex mirrors chosen for such purposes?
questions.answer:
(a) Positive; a convex mirror has f = +50 cm = +0.5 m.
(b) u = -4 m = -400 cm, f = +50 cm. 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/50 + 1/400 = (8 + 1)/400 = 9/400, so v = 400/9 = +44.4 cm (virtual, behind the mirror).
(c) m = -v/u = -(44.4)/(-400) = +0.111, so the image is erect and about one-ninth the size.
(d) A convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image and a very wide field of view, letting the shopkeeper watch a large area - ideal for security.
questions.explanation: Convex mirror numerical plus reasoning for its use.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A coin appears to be raised when viewed through water because of refraction. The refractive index of water is 1.33 and light travels at 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum.
(a) Define refractive index in terms of speed.
(b) Find the speed of light in water.
(c) When light goes from water into air, does it bend toward or away from the normal?
(d) Does the frequency of light change as it leaves the water?
questions.answer:
(a) Refractive index n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium.
(b) v = c/n = (3 x 10^8)/1.33 = 2.26 x 10^8 m/s.
(c) Going from water (denser) into air (rarer) the ray bends away from the normal.
(d) No; the frequency stays the same on refraction - only the speed and wavelength change.
questions.explanation: Refractive index, speed in medium, bending direction and constant frequency.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. An optician combines two thin lenses in contact: a convex lens of focal length 20 cm and a concave lens of focal length 40 cm.
(a) Find the power of each lens.
(b) Find the power of the combination.
(c) Find the focal length of the combination.
(d) Is the combination converging or diverging?
questions.answer:
(a) Convex: P1 = 1/0.20 = +5 D. Concave: P2 = 1/(-0.40) = -2.5 D.
(b) In contact powers add: P = P1 + P2 = 5 - 2.5 = +2.5 D.
(c) f = 1/P = 1/2.5 = 0.4 m = 40 cm.
(d) Since P is positive, the combination is converging.
questions.explanation: Powers of individual lenses, combination, focal length and nature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. An astronomical telescope is built with an objective of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 6 cm and used to view the Moon in normal adjustment.
(a) Which lens should have the longer focal length?
(b) Write the formula for the magnifying power in normal adjustment.
(c) Calculate the magnifying power.
(d) State the nature (real/virtual, erect/inverted) of the final image.
questions.answer:
(a) The objective should have the longer focal length (here 150 cm), the eyepiece the shorter (6 cm).
(b) M = fo/fe.
(c) M = 150/6 = 25.
(d) The final image seen through an astronomical telescope is virtual and inverted.
questions.explanation: Telescope focal-length choice, formula, numerical and image nature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A lens designer wants a converging lens using glass of refractive index 1.5. The chosen equiconvex shape has each surface of radius of curvature 20 cm.
(a) Write the lens maker's formula.
(b) Assign signs to R1 and R2 for an equiconvex lens.
(c) Calculate the focal length.
(d) What happens to the focal length if a higher-index glass is used?
questions.answer:
(a) 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2).
(b) For an equiconvex lens R1 = +20 cm and R2 = -20 cm.
(c) 1/f = (1.5 - 1)(1/20 - 1/(-20)) = 0.5 x (1/20 + 1/20) = 0.5 x (2/20) = 1/20, so f = +20 cm.
(d) A higher refractive index makes (n - 1) larger, so 1/f increases and the focal length becomes shorter (the lens converges more strongly).
questions.explanation: Lens maker's formula, sign assignment, numerical and effect of index.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A ray of light travelling inside a glass block (refractive index 1.5) strikes the glass-air surface at various angles.
(a) Calculate the critical angle for this glass-air surface.
(b) If the ray strikes the surface at 30 degrees, what happens?
(c) If it strikes at 50 degrees, what happens?
(d) Name a device that uses this effect to turn light through 90 degrees.
questions.answer:
(a) sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C = 41.8 degrees (about 42 degrees).
(b) At 30 degrees, which is less than the critical angle, the ray is mostly refracted out into the air (with partial reflection); it passes through the surface.
(c) At 50 degrees, greater than the critical angle, the ray undergoes total internal reflection and stays inside the glass.
(d) A totally reflecting (45-45-90) prism, as used in a periscope or binoculars.
questions.explanation: Critical angle numerical and comparison of two incidence angles, plus a device.
